questions.stem: The angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circumference of a circle is:
questions.explanation: This is the angle in a semicircle theorem: the angle is always a right angle, $90°$. It is a special case of the angle at the centre theorem, since the diameter makes a straight angle of $180°$ at the centre, and half of $180°$ is $90°$.

distractorRationale.a: Would only arise in a specific isosceles right-angled construction
distractorRationale.b: The angle of an equilateral triangle, not related to a diameter
distractorRationale.d: This is the angle at the centre, not at the circumference

questions.stem: An arc of a circle subtends an angle of $120°$ at the centre. What angle does the same arc subtend at the circumference?
questions.explanation: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc, so the angle at the circumference is $120° \div 2 = 60°$.

distractorRationale.c: Assumed the two angles are equal
distractorRationale.d: Doubled instead of halving, reversing the direction of the theorem

questions.stem: In a cyclic quadrilateral one of the angles is $85°$. Find the angle opposite it.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, so they add to $180°$. The opposite angle is $180° - 85° = 95°$.

distractorRationale.a: Subtracted from 90°, treating the angles as complementary
distractorRationale.b: Assumed opposite angles are equal, which is true for a parallelogram, not a cyclic quadrilateral
distractorRationale.d: Subtracted from 360°

questions.stem: What is the angle between a tangent to a circle and the radius drawn to the point of contact?

options.text: It depends on the size of the circle

questions.explanation: A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point, and at that point it is perpendicular to the radius, so the angle is $90°$. This holds for every circle, whatever its radius.

distractorRationale.a: No construction in the theorem produces 45°
distractorRationale.b: Confuses this with angles in an equilateral triangle
distractorRationale.d: The result is independent of the radius

questions.stem: Points $C$ and $D$ lie on the same side of chord $AB$ in a circle. If angle $ACB = 35°$, find angle $ADB$.
questions.explanation: Angles subtended by the same arc in the same segment are equal. Since $C$ and $D$ are on the same side of $AB$, both angles stand on the same arc, so angle $ADB = 35°$.

distractorRationale.a: Halved the angle, confusing this with the angle at the centre theorem
distractorRationale.c: Doubled the angle, which would give the angle at the centre
distractorRationale.d: Subtracted from 180°, which applies to angles in opposite segments

questions.stem: An arc subtends an angle of $42°$ at the circumference of a circle. Find, in degrees, the angle it subtends at the centre. Give a number only.
questions.explanation: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc, so it is $2 \times 42° = 84°$. Note the direction of the theorem: the centre angle is the larger of the two.

questions.stem: According to the alternate segment theorem, the angle between a tangent and a chord drawn from the point of contact is equal to:

options.text: the angle in the alternate segment
the angle at the centre on the same chord
half the angle in the alternate segment
$90°$ minus the angle in the alternate segment

questions.explanation: The alternate segment theorem states that the tangent–chord angle equals the angle subtended by that chord in the segment on the other side of the chord. The two angles are exactly equal, with no halving or subtraction involved.

distractorRationale.b: The centre angle would be twice the angle in the alternate segment
distractorRationale.c: Confuses this with the angle at the centre theorem
distractorRationale.d: Would only be true in the special case of a right angle

questions.stem: In cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, angle $A = 3x$ and angle $C = 2x + 20°$. Find the value of $x$.
questions.explanation: Angles $A$ and $C$ are opposite in a cyclic quadrilateral, so they add to $180°$: $3x + 2x + 20 = 180$. That gives $5x = 160$ and $x = 32°$. Checking, angle $A = 96°$ and angle $C = 84°$, which sum to $180°$.

distractorRationale.a: Used 120° as the sum of the opposite angles
distractorRationale.c: Solved $5x = 180$, forgetting to subtract the 20
distractorRationale.d: Gave the size of angle C rather than the value of x

questions.stem: $O$ is the centre of a circle and $A$ and $B$ are points on the circle. If angle $AOB = 80°$, find angle $OAB$.
questions.explanation: $OA$ and $OB$ are both radii, so triangle $OAB$ is isosceles and angles $OAB$ and $OBA$ are equal. The remaining angle sum is $180° - 80° = 100°$, shared equally, so angle $OAB = 50°$.

distractorRationale.a: Halved the angle at the centre instead of halving the remaining 100°
distractorRationale.c: Assumed the triangle is equilateral
distractorRationale.d: Gave the combined total of the two base angles

questions.stem: Two tangents from an external point $T$ touch a circle of centre $O$ at $A$ and $B$. If angle $ATB = 50°$, find angle $AOB$.
questions.explanation: The tangents meet the radii at right angles, so angles $OAT$ and $OBT$ are each $90°$. In quadrilateral $OATB$ the angles add to $360°$, so $90 + 90 + 50 + \angle AOB = 360$, giving angle $AOB = 130°$.

distractorRationale.a: Doubled the angle at T, applying the wrong theorem
distractorRationale.b: Used a triangle angle sum of 180° for a four-sided figure
distractorRationale.d: Subtracted 50 from 190 by arithmetic slip
